title: Korean BBQ Galbi
author: Robert Carr
description: LA-style beef short ribs in a pear, soy, and rice-wine marinade, grilled over two heat zones on stainless-steel grates and finished with a reserved sesame glaze.
cookTime: 15 minutes, allowing 3 to 5 minutes per batch
additionalTime: 8 to 18 hours marinating, plus 3 minutes resting
yield: About 10 to 12 flanken-cut strips, depending on the butcher
equipment: Gas grill with stainless-steel grates and independently controlled burners
Food-safe zipper bag or shallow nonreactive dish
Small covered container for reserved marinade
Wire rack over a rimmed baking sheet or colander
ingredients: 3 pounds (1.36 kg) LA-style flanken-cut beef short ribs, sliced across the bones 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick
180 g Korean or Asian pear, peeled and cored, about 1 medium pear
120 g yellow onion, about 1 small onion, roughly chopped
30 g garlic, about 8 large cloves, peeled
15 g fresh ginger, peeled, about 1 tablespoon finely grated
3/4 cup (180 mL) standard-strength brewed soy sauce
1/2 cup (120 mL) water
1/4 cup (60 mL) mirin or Korean mirim
1/4 cup (60 mL) dry sake or Korean rice wine
1/4 cup packed (55 g) brown sugar
1 1/2 tablespoons (30 g) rice syrup or honey
2 tablespoons (30 mL) toasted sesame oil, divided: 1 1/2 tablespoons for the marinade and 1 1/2 teaspoons for the glaze
4 medium scallions (50 g), whites and light greens for the marinade, dark greens sliced for garnish
1 1/2 teaspoons (4 g) freshly ground black pepper
1/2 teaspoon (2 g) MSG, optional
1 tablespoon (15 mL) neutral high-heat oil, for the ribs
2 teaspoons (10 mL) unseasoned rice vinegar, for the glaze
1 1/2 tablespoons (12 g) toasted sesame seeds, for garnish
Steamed short-grain rice, optional for serving
Red leaf lettuce, optional for wraps
Kimchi, optional for serving

groceryIngredients.note: Peeled and cored weight; about 1 medium pear; Bosc pear or tart apple can substitute
Standard-strength brewed soy sauce, not sweet or dark soy sauce
Total for marinade and finishing glaze

instructions: Inspect the 3 pounds of short ribs for bone-saw fragments and remove any with a damp disposable towel. Trim hard exterior fat and loose tissue while leaving marbling and soft fat edges. Do not rinse or soak the raw beef.
Blend 180 g peeled and cored pear, 120 g onion, 30 g garlic, and 15 g peeled ginger into a smooth puree.

Add 3/4 cup soy sauce, 1/2 cup water, 1/4 cup mirin, 1/4 cup sake, 55 g brown sugar, 30 g rice syrup or honey, the white and light-green parts of 4 scallions, 1 1/2 teaspoons black pepper, and the optional 1/2 teaspoon MSG. Blend until combined and the sugar dissolves, then stir in 1 1/2 tablespoons toasted sesame oil. Refrigerate the sliced dark scallion greens for garnish.
Before adding any beef, measure 1/2 cup (120 mL) of the clean marinade into a separate covered container and refrigerate it for the glaze.

Place the 3 pounds of ribs in a food-safe bag or shallow nonreactive dish and coat with the remaining marinade, working it between the strips. Seal or cover and refrigerate for 8 to 18 hours, turning once if practical. Keep the full pear marinade to 24 hours or less.

On cooking day, pour the reserved 1/2 cup clean marinade into a small saucepan. Simmer until reduced to about 1/4 cup (55 to 65 mL), stirring and watching closely; it should lightly coat a spoon. Off the heat, stir in 2 teaspoons rice vinegar and the remaining 1 1/2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil.

Preheat the gas grill on high with the lid closed for about 15 minutes, until the chamber reaches 500 to 550 degrees F (260 to 288 degrees C). Clean the stainless-steel grates, then set a direct cooking zone to medium-high, about 450 to 500 degrees F (232 to 260 degrees C), with an adjacent unlit or low zone.

While the grill preheats, lift the ribs onto a rack over a tray or into a colander and drain for 10 minutes. Blot away thick clumps of pear and onion, leaving a thin seasoning film. Discard the used raw marinade. Lightly coat both sides of the ribs with 1 tablespoon neutral high-heat oil total.

Grill the ribs in uncrowded batches over the direct zone, leaving room to move them away from flare-ups. Leave the first side undisturbed for 75 to 90 seconds. If the meat resists lifting, give it another 10 to 20 seconds before trying again.

Flip and cook the second side for 60 to 90 seconds. Continue turning every 20 to 30 seconds as needed for even browning. Expect about 3 to 5 minutes total per batch of 1/4-inch ribs. Move any strips surrounded by flames to the cool zone and lower the burner before resuming direct grilling.

During only the final 20 to 30 seconds per side, brush on a very thin layer of the reduced glaze. Divide the glaze among the batches. Look for a deep brown surface with small charred edges; move the ribs to the cooler zone if the sugars blacken before the meat is done.

Check for at least 145 degrees F (63 degrees C) in the thickest meat by inserting an instant-read thermometer horizontally, away from bone. Transfer to a clean platter and rest each batch for at least 3 minutes before cutting or eating. Do not tightly wrap the ribs in foil.

Scatter the 1 1/2 tablespoons toasted sesame seeds and reserved dark scallion greens over the ribs. Use kitchen shears to cut between the bone sections into bite-size pieces. Serve with steamed short-grain rice, red leaf lettuce, and kimchi if desired.
notes: Choose LA-style flanken ribs cut across several bones, ideally 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick; 1/8-inch (3 mm) strips cook faster. Thick English-cut ribs need butterflying into thin sheets before this quick grilling method will work.

The preferred marinade window is 8 to 18 hours. A 1 to 2 hour marinade is a workable quick option; 24 hours is the upper limit for the complete pear mixture. Keep the meat refrigerated throughout marinating.

For a staged 24 to 48 hour schedule, first make the marinade without the 180 g pear and 15 g ginger. Reserve 1/2 cup of that clean base before it touches beef and refrigerate separately for the glaze. Marinate the ribs in the remaining base, adding the freshly pureed pear and ginger only for the final 4 to 8 hours. The reserved glaze in this variation will be less fruity; never take glaze from the meat's marinade.

Bosc pear or tart apple can replace Asian pear by weight. Do not replace the pear with an equal amount of kiwi or fresh pineapple for an overnight marinade; their tenderizing action can make the surface mushy.
For less sweetness, use 35 g brown sugar and 15 g rice syrup or honey. For less salt, replace the 180 mL soy sauce with 150 mL soy sauce and increase the water from 120 to 150 mL.
To replace the sake and mirin, use 90 mL water plus 30 mL pear or apple juice in place of their combined 120 mL, and add 10 g brown sugar. This is in addition to the base recipe's water and sugar.

Use certified gluten-free tamari and check the other condiments if a gluten-free version is needed. For sesame-free preparation, omit the sesame oil and seeds and use a little additional neutral oil when finishing.

If the ribs stick, allow more searing time before lifting. If they steam, drain more thoroughly and cook smaller batches. If the glaze turns bitter or black, reduce the heat, use the cool zone, and brush it on later.

Optional ginger dipping sauce, separate from the main ingredient and grocery lists: whisk 2 tablespoons soy sauce, 2 tablespoons rice vinegar, 1 tablespoon plus 1 teaspoon water, 1 tablespoon finely grated pear (15 g), and 2 teaspoons rice syrup or honey (12 g). Stir in 2 tablespoons finely grated ginger (30 g), 2 tablespoons sliced scallion (10 g), 2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil, 1 tablespoon neutral oil, and 1 teaspoon toasted sesame seeds. Add 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon gochugaru if desired. Let stand for 15 minutes and serve sparingly, about 1 to 2 teaspoons per wrap.
Other optional table accompaniments include perilla leaves, ssamjang, sliced garlic, and fresh green chile. Side dishes and the optional dipping sauce are excluded from the nutrition estimates.

The marinade can be made up to 2 days ahead and refrigerated separately. Refrigerate cooked ribs within 2 hours, or within 1 hour when the surrounding temperature exceeds 90 degrees F (32 degrees C). Use refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat in a skillet with a little water as needed, until the meat reaches 165 degrees F (74 degrees C); use temperature rather than a fixed reheating time.

Nutrition is the supplied research report's rough estimate for one of six servings of galbi and glaze. Rib marbling, bone weight, trim, and discarded marinade make actual calories and sodium highly variable; these values are not a measured analysis.

Project adaptation of the supplied Korean BBQ Galbi research report, with original recipe wording. The report draws on Hooni Kim's My Korea, Maangchi's LA galbi (https://www.maangchi.com/recipe/la-galbi), and Sasha Marx's Serious Eats recipe based on Beverly Kim's marinade (https://www.seriouseats.com/grilled-beef-galbi-korean-style-marinated-short-ribs). The linked recipe is one influence, not the sole source of this formulation.
Cooking, resting, and reheating temperatures follow USDA food-safety guidance: https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/steps-keep-food-safe
